## Human-centric, computer-enabled research

The ultimate purpose of research is human understanding and betterment of human lives.  Machines and AI are powerful tools toward those goals.  Research results should be provided in a form that is easy for machines to digest as well as in a form that is easy for humans to read and understand.

I make my code and data publicly available so that other researchers can easily incorporate them into their own work.  Everything in my published papers is, at a minimum, reviewed and revised by myself and my coauthors (who are human).  AI tool usage is acknowledged in every publication with a clear indication of what it was used for.


## Openness in research and teaching

I try to practice scientific research in the open as suggested in
[Reinventing Discovery](/2011/11/10/book-review-reinventing-discovery.html)
and scientific teaching in the open as suggested by 
[Greg Wilson](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1e26rp6qPbA).
The idea is that openness enables massive collaboration, and collaboration
leads to better tools, materials, and results.

 - I post my [teaching materials on Github](/teaching.html)
 - I post my [research code on Github](https://github.com/ketch)
 - I have published some grant proposals on Figshare: 
    * [Wave Propagation for Next-Generation Supercomputers](https://dx.doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.639182), 
    * [Positive Numerical Solution of Differential Equations](https://dx.doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.639184), 
    * [High Performance Computing and High-Level Programming Concepts for Hyperbolic PDE Codes](https://dx.doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.639183)
 - I participate in the [Stack Exchange for Scientific Computing](https://scicomp.stackexchange.com)
 - I participate in the [Stack Exchange for Academia](https://academia.stackexchange.com)

See also: [posts tagged with **open-science**](/posts.html#category=open-science)


## Scientific software and reproducibility

Software development is a critical part of science and deserves to be treated
as such.  Virtually all published science depends on numerous software tools.
I subscribe to the principles outlined in the 
[Science Code Manifesto](https://web.archive.org/web/20141218091613/http://sciencecodemanifesto.org/)
and the [Reproducible Research Standard](https://doi.org/10.1109/MCSE.2009.19).

To ensure the accuracy and reliability of computational scientific results,
it is essential that we strive for a standard of reproducibility.  To this
end, I make all code used in my papers [publicly available](https://github.com/ketch).  Where reasonable,
I try to make the code well-documented and easy to use.

See also: [posts tagged with **reproducible-research**](/posts.html#category=reproducible-research)


## Scientific publishing and journal pricing

I believe that publishing publicly-funded scientific research should not
be a profit-motivated activity.  Charges for access to scientific publications
should be kept to a minimum.  I primarily publish my own work in relatively
inexpensive but highly respected journals run by non-profit professional 
societies ([SIAM](https://www.siam.org) and the [AMS](https://www.ams.org)).
I am a signatory to the [Cost of Knowledge](http://thecostofknowledge.com)
(Elsevier Boycott).  I do not support gold open access (i.e., author-pay) journals,
for reasons outlined 
[here](/2011/12/16/in-defense-of-submission-in-scientific.html).
I place preprints of all my manuscripts on the [arXiv](https://www.arxiv.org)
when I submit them for publication.  Where allowed by the publisher, I put the
final version of my published papers on my site, downloadable from
[my publications page](/publications.html).
